'''Michele Karen Dougherty''' (born 1962)<ref name=whoswho/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sciencephoto.com/media/589826/view| title=Michele Dougherty, British astrophysicist| date=2008| access-date=27 September 2016| publisher=[[Science Photo Library]]}}</ref> is a British scientist. She is [[professor]] of [[space physics]] at [[Imperial College London]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/people/m.dougherty |title=Professor Michele Dougherty, Professor of Space Physics, Imperial College London |archive-date=2012-03-06|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306040735/http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/people/m.dougherty}}</ref><ref name=tls>{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b087qjcw|title=Michele Dougherty interview|publisher=[[BBC Radio 4]]|website=bbc.co.uk|year=2017|first=Jim|last=Al-Khalili|author-link=Jim Al-Khalili}} from [[The Life Scientific]] {{blockquote|The Cassini mission into deep space has sent back some wonderful colour images of Saturn. It's witnessed raging storms, flown between its enigmatic rings and revealed seven new moons. And, thanks in no small part to Professor Michele Dougherty - it's made some astonishing discoveries.}}</ref> and the sixteenth [[Astronomer Royal]].<ref name="Royal">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c741lll88q5o|title=UK gets first female Astronomer Royal in 350 years|work=BBC News|date=30 July 2025}}</ref> She is leading uncrewed exploratory missions to [[Saturn]] and [[Jupiter]], and is [[principal investigator]] for J-MAG – a [[magnetometer]] aboard the [[European Space Agency]]'s [[Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer]].<ref name=tls/>

She was appointed to Executive Chair of the [[Science and Technology Facilities Council]] in September 2024,<ref>{{cite web |title=Executive chair for STFC appointed |url=https://www.ukri.org/news/executive-chair-for-stfc-appointed/ |website=www.ukri.org |publisher=UK Research and Innovation |access-date=9 September 2024 |date=5 September 2024}}</ref> and was appointed [[Astronomer Royal]] in July 2025, making her the first woman in that office.<ref name="Royal" /> She was elected to serve as President of the [[Institute of Physics]] from October 2025 <ref>{{cite web |title=President-elect: Professor Michele Dougherty CBE FRS FInstP FRAS FRSSAf |url=https://www.iop.org/about/governance/council/michele-dougherty |website=Institute of Physics |access-date=9 September 2024}}</ref> but stepped down in January 2026 citing concerns of a conflict of interest with her role at STFC.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Banks |first=Michael |date=2026-01-29 |title=Michele Dougherty steps aside as president of the Institute of Physics |url=https://physicsworld.com/michele-dougherty-steps-aside-as-president-of-the-institute-of-physics/ |access-date=2026-03-04 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Michele Dougherty became interested in space when she was ten years old, when her father built a 10-inch telescope through which she saw the moons of Jupiter and Saturn.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/people/doughertym|title=Michele Dougherty {{!}} People - NASA Solar System Exploration|website=NASA Solar System Exploration|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref> Dougherty learnt no science at secondary school, as the one she attended, chosen because 'I thought, I want to go [to the same school] with my friends', did not teach science. Nonetheless, her ability at mathematics led to her admission to read for a science degree (which 'was like learning a new language') at the [[University of Natal]] in South Africa,<ref name="Royal" /> where she was awarded a [[PhD]] degree in 1988 for research on [[Wave–particle duality|wave-particle interactions]] in [[Dispersion (optics)|dispersive]] and [[Anisotropy|anisotropic media]].<ref name=phd>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Michele|last=Karen Dougherty |title=Wave-particle interactions in dispersive and anisotropic media
 |publisher=University of Natal |date=1988 |oclc=890036806}}</ref>

==Career==
Dougherty left South Africa for a fellowship in Germany, working on applied mathematics, before moving to Imperial College London in 1991.<ref name=":0" /> She was appointed a Professor of Space Physics in 2004 and teaches undergraduates alongside her research.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/people/m.dougherty|title=Home - Professor Michele Dougherty|website=www.imperial.ac.uk|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref> She was head of the [[Blackett Laboratory|Department of Physics]] at [[Imperial College London]] from 2018 to 2024.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://wwwf.imperial.ac.uk/blog/announcements/2017/04/27/head-of-department-of-physics/|title=Head of Department of Physics|date=2017-04-27|work=Announcements|access-date=2017-12-30|language=en-US|archive-date=2019-06-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190618012311/http://wwwf.imperial.ac.uk/blog/announcements/2017/04/27/head-of-department-of-physics/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Royal" />

Dougherty is the principal investigator for two major space missions; the NASA [[Cassini–Huygens|Cassini]] spacecraft that orbited Saturn and the ESA [[Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer|JUICE spacecraft]] that will orbit Jupiter's largest moon, Ganymede.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2014/research-professorships/|title=Top scientists receive Royal Society Research Professorships to fund long-term UK research|website=royalsociety.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref>

Dougherty's work led to the discovery of an [[atmosphere]] containing water and [[hydrocarbon]]s around Saturn's moon [[Enceladus]] — opening up new possibilities in the search for [[extraterrestrial life]].<ref name=frs>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117103041/https://royalsociety.org/people/michele-dougherty-11354/ |archive-date=2015-11-17 |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/michele-dougherty-11354/ |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London |title=Professor Michele Dougherty FRS |author=Anon |year=2012 |website=royalsociety.org }} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{blockquote|“All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]].” --{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=2016-03-09 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925220834/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archive-date=September 25, 2015 }}}}</ref><ref name="GladstoneWaite2002">{{cite journal|last1=Gladstone|first1=G. Dougherty is distinguished by the [[Royal Society]] "for her scientific leadership of the international [[NASA]]-ESA-[[Italian Space Agency|ASI]] [[Cassini-Huygens mission]] to Saturn and its moons".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ralspace.stfc.ac.uk/Pages/Cassini-sees-new-objects-blazing-trails-in-Saturn-ring.aspx |title=Cassini sees new objects blazing trails in Saturn ring |date=2012-04-24 |access-date=2019-08-20 |website=RAL Space |publisher=[[Science and Technology Facilities Council]]}}</ref> As principal investigator of the operation, data collection and analysis of observations from the magnetic field instrument on board the Cassini spacecraft, she strongly contributed to improve our understanding of Saturn and the [[Moons of Saturn]].<ref name="cutlerphd">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=Imperial College London|title=The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability on the Kronian magnetopause|first= Jack|last=Cutler|date=2014|hdl=10044/1/41877}} {{open access}}</ref><ref name="wentphd">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=Imperial College London|title=Magnetic field and plasma in Saturn's near space environment|first= Daniel Robert|last=Went|date=2011|oclc=930625731|hdl=10044/1/9066}} {{open access}}</ref><ref name="ArridgeEastwood2015">{{cite journal|last1=Arridge|first1=C. L.|title=Origin of Saturn's aurora: Simultaneous observations by Cassini and the Hubble Space Telescope|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics|volume=113|issue=A9|article-number=2008JA013257 |year=2008|pages=n/a |issn=0148-0227|doi=10.1029/2008JA013257|bibcode = 2008JGRA..113.9209B |url=https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/95541/1/jgra19446.pdf|hdl=2027.42/95541 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="EspinosaDougherty2000">{{cite journal|last1=Espinosa|first1=Stéphane A.|last2=Dougherty|first2=Michele K.|title=Periodic perturbations in Saturn's magnetic field|journal=[[Geophysical Research Letters]]|volume=27|issue=17|year=2000|pages=2785–2788|doi=10.1029/2000GL000048|bibcode = 2000GeoRL..27.2785E |s2cid=123083913 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Dougherty cites the flybys of Saturn's moons as a highlight of her career; convincing the NASA spacecraft team to make a closer than usual approach “I watched the data coming back with my heart in my mouth because if we had messed up no one would have ever believed me again!".<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/newsandeventspggrp/imperialcollege/newssummary/news_31-10-2014-12-34-18|title=Professor Michele Dougherty talks about space missions and her first telescope|last=Gallagher|first=Laura|date=2014-10-31|work=Imperial College London|access-date=2017-12-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150919104411/http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/newsandeventspggrp/imperialcollege/newssummary/news_31-10-2014-12-34-18|archive-date=2015-09-19|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Before working on the Cassini-Huygens spacecraft, Dougherty was involved in the magnetometer team for the Jupiter analysis of the [[Ulysses (spacecraft)|Ulysses mission]]. She was also Guest Investigator on the NASA Jupiter System Data Analysis Program as part of the [[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo uncrewed spacecraft]].<ref name="homepage">{{cite web|url=http://www.sp.ph.ic.ac.uk/~mkd/oldwelcome.html|title=Michele Dougherty FRS Home Page|website=ic.ac.uk|location=London|author=Anon|year=2000}}</ref>

Dougherty regularly delivers public lectures and appears on national media.<ref>{{Citation|last=euronews (in English)|title=Cassini scientist Michele Dougherty from Imperial College London talks Saturn, Enceladus and Titan|date=2017-09-12|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mZzqdLH5phE |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211215/mZzqdLH5phE |archive-date=2021-12-15 |url-status=live|access-date=2017-12-30}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://live.newscientist.com/speakers/michele-dougherty|title=Michele Dougherty|work=New Scientist Live 2017|access-date=2017-12-30|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.royalalberthall.com/tickets/events/2018/imperial-college-talks-first-saturn-then-jupiter/|title=Imperial College Talks: First Saturn, then Jupiter — Royal Albert Hall|website=Royal Albert Hall|language=en-GB|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ukseds.org/nssc2016/?p=speakers|title=UKSEDS National Student Space Conference|website=UKSEDS.org|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref> She was one of the guest scientists interviewed on [[Jim Al-Khalili]]'s radio programme ''The Life Scientific''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b087qjcw|title=Michele Dougherty on Saturn, The Life Scientific - BBC Radio 4|website=BBC|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref>

In July 2025, Dougherty was appointed the UK's [[Astronomer Royal]]. She is the first woman in the post's 350-year history.<ref name="Royal" />

==Awards and honours==
In 2007, Dougherty won the [[Appleton Medal and Prize|Chree Medal and Prize]] from the Institute of Physics for "her contributions to the field of planetary magnetic fields and atmospheres and their interactions with the solar wind".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/silver/appleton/medallists/page_38521.html|title=Appleton medal recipients|last=Physics|first=Institute of|website=www.iop.org|language=en-GB|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref>

Dougherty won the 2008 [[Hughes Medal]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/awards/hughes-medal/ |title=List of 21st century winners of the Hughes Medal|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref> of the [[Royal Society]] "for innovative use of magnetic field data that led to discovery of an atmosphere around one of [[Saturn]]'s moons and the way it revolutionised our view of the role of planetary moons in the [[Solar System]]". She is the second woman ever to receive such an accolade, 102 years after [[Hertha Ayrton]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Women at Imperial College; Past, Present and Future|last=Barrett|first=Anne|publisher=World Scientific Europe|year=2017|isbn=978-1786342621|pages=215}}</ref>

Dougherty was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 2012<ref name="frs" /> and was recognized by the UK [[Science Council]] as one of the 100 top UK living scientists.<ref name="congrats">{{cite web|url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/newsandeventspggrp/imperialcollege/naturalsciences/physics/newssummary/news_14-1-2014-13-56-47|title= Congratulations Professor Michele Dougherty - named in top 100 Scientists|website=imperial.ac.uk|first=Caroline|last=Jackson|year=2014}}</ref> She was awarded a prestigious Royal Society Research Professorship in 2014.<ref name=":1" />

Dougherty was awarded the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] for [[geophysics]] in 2017, the fifth woman ever to receive the honour.<ref name="ras_gold_medal">{{cite web|title=RAS honours leading astronomers and geophysicists|url=http://www.ras.org.uk/news-and-press/2943-ras-honours-leading-astronomers-and-geophysicists-2017|publisher=Royal Astronomical Society|access-date=17 January 2017|date=11 January 2017|author=Anon|website=ras.org.uk}}</ref>

Dougherty has contributed significantly to the UK space sector, and chaired the Science Programme Advisory Committee of the UK Space Agency between 2014 and 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://spaceref.com/europe/new-chairs-for-two-uk-space-agency-advisory-committees.html|title=New Chairs for two UK Space Agency Advisory Committees - SpaceRef|website=spaceref.com|date=5 April 2013 |language=en|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref> She was made [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire|Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE)]] in the [[2018 New Year Honours]] for "services to UK Physical Science Research".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/new-years-honours-list-2018 |title=2018 New Year Honours List|website=www.gov.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/britains-first-astronaut-and-professor-of-space-physics-receive-new-years-honours|title=Britain's first astronaut and Professor of Space Physics receive New Year's honours - GOV.UK|website=www.gov.uk|language=en|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref> Dougherty won the 2018 [[Richard Glazebrook Medal and Prize]] from the [[Institute of Physics]]. In 2019, Dougherty was named a Fellow of the [[American Geophysical Union]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://eos.org/agu-news/2019-class-of-agu-fellows-announced|title=2019 Class of AGU Fellows Announced|website=Eos|date=15 August 2019 |language=en-US|access-date=2019-08-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Celebrating the 2019 Class of Fellows|url=https://eos.org/agu-news/celebrating-the-2019-class-of-fellows|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Eos|date=12 December 2019 |language=en-US}}</ref>

In February 2026, Dougherty guested on BBC radio’s [[Desert Island Discs]] when she said the one record she would save from the waves is Elgar’s Cello Concerto in E Minor because it features the instrument she feels makes the most beautiful music.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m002qrfh
| title=Desert Island Discs | publisher=BBC R4 | date=1 February 2026 | accessdate=1 February 2026}}</ref>
